title: Ancient 7‑Metre Sea Creature: Weighing a Tonne, Living 400+ Years Since 1626【BBC Wildlife】
body:
A team of marine scientists has finally cracked the age mystery of the Greenland shark, confirming that the species can live for four centuries or more. Using cutting‑edge radiocarbon dating of eye‑lens proteins, researchers estimate that some individuals swimming the icy waters of the North Atlantic today were born in the early 1600s—making them older than the United States and even the city of New York. The findings, published this week, reshape our understanding of shark longevity, deep‑sea ecology, and the challenges of conserving one of the ocean’s most enigmatic apex predators.

The Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus) is already famous for its massive size—adults can reach up to seven metres in length and weigh close to a tonne. Yet its slow growth rate, measured in mere centimetres per decade, has long hinted at an extraordinary lifespan. Previous estimates, based on indirect methods such as growth rings in vertebrae, suggested ages of several hundred years but carried large uncertainties. The new study, led by researchers from the University of Iceland and the University of Washington, employed a technique originally developed for dating ancient whale eyes. By extracting and analysing the stable isotopic composition of the proteins in the sharks’ eye lenses—structures that, like tree rings, record chemical signatures over an animal’s life—the team could calculate the exact year each shark was born.

The results were striking. Of the 28 sharks sampled, the oldest individual was estimated to be 392 ± 120 years old, while the median age of the sample set hovered around 250 years. This places the Greenland shark among the longest‑lived vertebrates on the planet, rivaling the bowhead whale and certain tortoise species. The researchers caution, however, that the wide confidence intervals reflect both natural variability and the challenges of working with deep‑sea specimens. Nevertheless, the data provide the most robust age estimates to date and confirm that these sharks have been silently patrolling the Arctic for centuries.

Understanding such extreme longevity has profound implications for marine biology and conservation. Long‑lived species typically exhibit low reproductive rates; Greenland sharks mature very slowly—potentially not until they are 150 years old—and produce few offspring. This life history makes them especially vulnerable to overfishing, bycatch, and habitat disturbance. While the species is not a target of commercial fisheries, it is occasionally caught in nets targeting cod and other Arctic fish, and its meat is sometimes sold as “fisk.” The new age data underscore the urgency of implementing protective measures, as the loss of even a handful of mature individuals could have outsized effects on population stability.

The study also opens new avenues for researching other deep‑sea organisms whose ages have remained elusive. Radiocarbon dating of eye lenses could be applied to species such as the frilled shark or the giant squid, offering insights into the hidden timelines of ecosystems that are otherwise difficult to study. Moreover, the findings challenge prevailing assumptions about metabolic rates and aging. Greenland sharks thrive in near‑freezing waters, a condition that appears to slow cellular processes and extend lifespan—a phenomenon that may inform broader scientific inquiries into longevity and climate adaptation.

Looking ahead, researchers plan to expand their sample size and explore genetic markers that could corroborate the radiocarbon findings. They also aim to map the sharks’ migratory patterns using satellite tagging, linking age data with movement ecology to better predict how climate change might impact this ancient species. As the Arctic continues to warm and human activity intensifies, the Greenland shark stands as a living archive of centuries of environmental change. Deciphering its long life not only enriches our knowledge of marine biodiversity but also highlights the delicate balance required to preserve a creature that has witnessed the rise and fall of empires beneath the waves.
